questions.q: How is a formal method best defined?
o: A way of writing software quickly without documentation
A branch of software engineering and computer science in which programs are argued about and analysed using mathematical and formal techniques
A testing method that runs many test cases
A programming language for embedded systems
questions.e: A formal method is a branch of both software engineering and computer science in which we argue about and analyse computer programs using mathematical and formal techniques; 'formal' means definite, orderly or methodical.

questions.q: Formal methods are used for three main purposes. Which set correctly lists them?
o: Specify the system, verify the system, and construct a correct program
Design the user interface, database and network
questions.e: Formal methods are used to specify a system (define the meaning of what it should do), to verify it (prove a written program fulfils its specification), and to construct a program that is correct.

questions.q: In the context of formal methods, what does it mean to 'verify' a system?
o: To define what the system is supposed to do
To prove, once the program is written, whether it fulfils the specification it was supposed to meet
To draw a flowchart of the system
To run the system on real hardware
questions.e: Verification means proving, once a program has been written, whether it fulfils the actual specification it was supposed to satisfy; specification, by contrast, defines the meaning of what the system should do.

questions.q: The Therac-25 is cited as a notorious software bug. What kind of system was it and what went wrong?
o: An aircraft autopilot that crashed planes
A computerised radiation therapy machine that delivered radiation overdoses and killed people
A telephone switching system that failed
questions.e: The Therac-25 was a computerised radiation therapy machine; due to a software bug the controller could not stop the radiation, and it killed several people through radiation overdoses (1985-87).

questions.q: The AT&T long-distance network breakdown of 1990 was caused by which kind of software fault?
o: An ill-placed break statement in the code
An integer overflow in a counter
questions.e: The 1990 AT&T long-distance breakdown was caused by an ill-placed break statement in the code, which brought down about one third of the entire American network for more than 9 hours.

questions.q: The Patriot Missile failure during the Gulf War, which failed to intercept a Scud missile and led to 28 deaths, is an example of what?
o: A software defect with fatal consequences
questions.e: The Patriot Missile failure (1991) was due to a software defect: the missile failed to track and intercept an incoming Scud, which struck American troops in barracks, killing 28 people.

questions.q: The Pentium (FDIV) bug of 1994 caused which kind of error?
o: Floating-point calculation errors due to an error in the microprocessor's microcode
Memory leaks in the operating system
questions.e: The Pentium bug was a software error in the microcode of the Pentium microprocessor that resulted in floating-point calculation errors, forcing Intel to recall the processors at huge cost.

questions.q: Which famous quotation by Edsger Dijkstra highlights a fundamental limitation of testing?
o: "Premature optimization is the root of all evil."
"Testing can show the presence of errors, but not their absence."
"A program is never finished, only abandoned."
questions.e: Dijkstra's quotation 'Testing can show the presence of errors, but not their absence' captures the point that no number of test cases can guarantee that a program is free of errors.

questions.q: What is the difference between black box testing and white box testing?
o: Black box tests the program's structure; white box tests input versus output
Black box tests input versus output; white box tests the internal structure of the program (loops, conditions)
Both test only the user interface
Black box requires source code; white box does not
questions.e: Black box testing checks input versus output without regard to internal structure, whereas white box testing examines the structure of the program, such as testing loops and conditions.

questions.q: A formal method is said to have two parts. What are they?
o: A logical theory (for reasoning about specifications, properties and programs) and a structuring theory (which defines the elements being reasoned about)
questions.e: A formal method has two parts: a logical theory, the means by which one reasons about specifications, properties and programs (predicate calculus, logic, propositions), and a structuring theory, which defines the elements being reasoned about.

questions.q: In Dijkstra's urn game, two balls are drawn repeatedly. If the two balls are the same colour, one black ball is put in; if different colours, one white ball is returned. What happens to the total number of balls on each move?
questions.e: In each move two balls are taken out and one is returned, so the total number of balls decreases by 1 on every move; the game is therefore guaranteed to terminate with exactly one ball.

questions.q: In Dijkstra's urn game, what determines the colour of the final remaining ball?
o: The total number of balls at the start
The parity (even or odd) of the number of white balls
The colour of the first ball drawn
Whether there are more black or white balls
questions.e: The outcome depends on the parity of the white balls: an even number of white balls leaves a black final ball, and an odd number of white balls leaves a white final ball, because each move preserves the parity of the white balls.

questions.q: According to the 1996 report to President Clinton mentioned in the study of reliability, what was stated about software reliability?
o: We can write software that works 100% of the time
We know how to write software that works 95% of the time, but not software that works 100% of the time
Software reliability is impossible to measure
questions.e: The 1996 IT committee report stated that we know how to write software that works 95% of the time, but do not know how to write software that works 100% of the time it is used.

questions.q: What are the two software quality attributes that formal methods primarily aim to ensure?
questions.e: Formal methods are used to ensure that software is correct and reliable; these two attributes deal with software quality.

questions.q: Does applying formal methods mean programming part of the system?
o: Yes, formal methods replace ordinary programming
No, formal methods are used to verify the system's correctness, not to program part of it
Yes, but only the user interface
No, formal methods only apply to hardware
questions.e: Formal methods do not mean programming a part of the system; rather, they are used to verify the correctness of the system, and they are based on mathematical models.

questions.q: Formal methods are based on what kind of foundation?
questions.e: Formal methods are based on mathematical models; with the help of models we argue about and prove the correctness of the system, even though they are difficult to apply.

questions.q: How is a software specification defined?
o: A rough sketch of the user interface
A precise, unambiguous and complete statement of the requirements of a system, written so it can be used to predict how the system will behave
The compiled machine code of a program
questions.e: A software specification is a precise, unambiguous and complete statement of the requirements of a system (or program or process), written in such a way that it can be used to predict how the system will behave.

questions.q: In what notation are formal specifications expressed?
o: A mathematical notation with precisely defined vocabulary, syntax and semantics
A programming language such as C++
questions.e: Formal specifications are expressed in a mathematical notation with precisely defined vocabulary, syntax and semantics, which removes the ambiguity of natural language.

questions.q: What is the difference between the algebraic approach and the model-based approach to formal specification?
o: The algebraic approach uses state models; the model-based approach uses operations

The algebraic approach specifies a system by its operations and their relationships (for interface specification); the model-based approach specifies it by a state model built from sets and sequences (for behavioural specification)
Both approaches specify only the user interface
The algebraic approach is informal; the model-based approach is formal
questions.e: In the algebraic approach the system is specified in terms of its operations and their relationships and is used for interface specification, whereas in the model-based approach the system is specified as a state model built from mathematical constructs such as sets and sequences, with operations defined by state modifications, used for behavioural specification.

questions.q: In an algebraic specification, what is defined by the 'Signature' part?
o: The syntax of the interface to the abstract data type, including operation names, parameter lists and return types
An informal description to aid understanding
questions.e: The Signature part of an algebraic specification defines the syntax of the interface to the abstract data type, including the operations' names, parameter lists and return types. The Axioms part defines the semantics.

questions.q: In an algebraic specification, what do the 'Axioms' define?
o: The type name of the entity
The semantics of the operations, by defining axioms that characterise their behaviour
questions.e: The Axioms part defines the semantics of the operations by giving axioms that characterise their behaviour, whereas the Signature defines only the syntax of the interface.

questions.q: In algebraic specification, operations are divided into two categories. What are they?
o: Constructor operations (create or modify entities, e.g. Create, Update, Add) and inspection operations (evaluate attributes, e.g. Eval, Get)
questions.e: Operations are divided into constructor operations, which create or modify entities of the sort (e.g. Create, Update, Add), and inspection operations, which evaluate attributes of the sort (e.g. Eval or Get).

questions.q: For an algebraic stack specification, what is the signature of the push operation?
questions.e: The push operation takes a stack and an element and returns a stack: push: (Stack, Element) -> Stack. By comparison, top: (Stack) -> Element and isEmpty: (Stack) -> Boolean.

questions.q: In the algebraic stack specification, which axiom captures the fact that the top of a stack after a push is the pushed element?
questions.e: The axiom top(push(s, e)) = e states that the top of a stack immediately after pushing e is e itself; isEmpty(push(s,e)) = false states that pushing yields a non-empty stack.

questions.q: Which classes of formal methods are the model-based approaches?
questions.e: The model-based approaches include B, VDM and Z. Algebraic approaches include CASL, Act One, Larch and OBJ; process algebras include CSP and CCS.

questions.q: Which of the following is an algebraic-approach formal method?
questions.e: Algebraic approaches include CASL, Act One, Larch and OBJ, whereas Z, VDM and B are model-based approaches.

questions.q: The algebraic method of specification was originally designed for what purpose?
o: Specifying the behaviour of concurrent processes
The definition of abstract data type interfaces, defining the type by its operations rather than its representation
questions.e: The algebraic approach was originally designed to define abstract data type interfaces; in an abstract data type the type is defined by specifying the type operations rather than the type representation, using the relationships between the operations.

questions.q: Which is stated as a benefit of investing effort in formal specification early in development?
o: It removes the need for any coding
It reduces requirements errors by forcing detailed analysis, so incompleteness and inconsistencies can be discovered and resolved, reducing later rework
It guarantees the software will never fail
It eliminates the need for testing
questions.e: Formal specification involves more effort in the early phases, but this reduces requirements errors because it forces a detailed analysis of the requirements; incompleteness and inconsistencies can be discovered and resolved, so savings are made through reduced rework.

questions.q: Which of the following is a real-world application of formal specification?
o: The Paris metro line traffic system and the IBM CICS transaction system
questions.e: Applications of formal specification include the Paris metro line for traffic, IBM's CICS (Customer Information and Control System), the UK air traffic display information system, Tektronix oscilloscopes, and a clinical neutron medical system.

questions.q: A formal specification language contains which three parts?
questions.e: A formal specification is described as a language that contains three parts: syntax, semantics and proof theory.

questions.q: What are the qualities of a good formal specification?
questions.e: Good formal specifications are complete, consistent, unambiguous and adequate; a system cannot be expressed formally in a single step but requires a series of steps and refinements.

questions.q: Why is mathematical logic studied as the foundation of formal methods?
o: Because natural languages such as English are too ambiguous for precise reasoning
Because logic runs faster than natural language
Because natural language cannot be written down
questions.e: Logic is studied because natural languages such as English are too ambiguous; logic is a discipline that studies the precise formalisation of knowledge and reasoning and is all about unambiguous reasoning.

questions.q: How is a proposition defined?
o: A declarative statement that is either true or false, but not both, and whose value cannot change
A question that expects a yes/no answer
A command to perform an action
questions.e: A proposition is a declarative statement that results in either true or false; it must be one or the other and cannot be both, and its value is constant (cannot change).

questions.q: What is an atomic proposition?
o: A proposition that is always true
A proposition that cannot be broken down into simpler propositions and whose truth does not depend on any other proposition
A proposition joined by a connective
A proposition that is always false
questions.e: An atomic proposition is one that cannot be broken down into simpler propositions; its truth or falsity does not depend on the truth or falsity of any other proposition.

questions.q: What test can be applied to a statement to determine whether it is a proposition?
o: Prefix it with 'It is true that ...' and see whether the result makes grammatical sense
Check whether it contains a variable
See whether it ends in a question mark
questions.e: You can determine whether a statement is a proposition by prefixing it with 'It is true that ...' and seeing whether the result makes grammatical sense.

questions.q: Logical connectives are described as functions of what kind?
o: Functions from Booleans to Booleans, with finite domain and range
questions.e: Logical connectives are functions from Booleans to Booleans; their domain and range are finite sets, so they can be given precise meaning by enumerating all input/output combinations in a truth table.

questions.q: The conjunction of two propositions p and q, written p ∧ q, is true under what condition?
o: When at least one of p or q is true
When both p and q are true
When p is true and q is false
When both p and q are false
questions.e: The conjunction p ∧ q (p AND q) is true only when both p and q are true.

questions.q: The disjunction p ∨ q is true under what condition?
o: Only when both p and q are true
When either p is true, or q is true, or both are true
Only when exactly one of p, q is true
questions.e: The disjunction p ∨ q (p OR q) is true if either p is true, or q is true, or both p and q are true.

questions.q: If a formula contains n different atomic propositions, how many rows (lines) does its truth table have?
questions.e: Because each proposition can take one of two values (true or false), a formula with n different atomic propositions has 2^n different lines in its truth table.

questions.q: The negation connective ¬ differs from AND and OR in what way?
o: It is unary, taking only one argument
It cannot be put in a truth table
questions.e: Unlike AND and OR, which are binary (two arguments), negation (¬) is unary and takes only one argument; ¬p is true if p is false.

questions.q: The implication (conditional) p ⇒ q is false only in which case?
o: When p is false and q is true
When p is true and q is false
questions.e: The conditional p ⇒ q is only false when its left-hand side p is true while its right-hand side q is false; in all other cases it is true.

questions.q: The biconditional p ⇔ q (if and only if) is true under what condition?
o: When p and q are both true, or both false
Only when exactly one is true
questions.e: The biconditional p ⇔ q is true if p and q are both true, or if p and q are both false; if it is true, p and q are said to be logically equivalent.

questions.q: A proposition that is always true regardless of the truth values of its components is called what?
questions.e: A tautology is a proposition which is always true. A contradiction is always false, and a contingency is neither a tautology nor a contradiction.

questions.q: A proposition that is always false is called what?
questions.e: A contradiction is a proposition which is always false. A tautology is always true, and a contingency is neither.

questions.q: A proposition that is neither always true nor always false is called what?
questions.e: A contingency is a proposition that is neither a tautology (always true) nor a contradiction (always false).

questions.q: Two logical expressions are logically equivalent when?
o: They have the same truth value in all cases (equivalently, their biconditional is a tautology)
They have the same number of connectives
questions.e: Two statements are logically equivalent if their truth tables have the same truth values in all cases, or equivalently if the biconditional X ⇔ Y is a tautology.

questions.q: What are the two methods given for proving that two propositions are logically equivalent?
questions.e: Two propositions can be proved logically equivalent using truth tables (checking all combinations) or using logical deductions (constructing a proof from already-established equivalences).

questions.q: The double negative property states which equivalence?
questions.e: The double negative property states that ¬(¬p) ≡ p; negating a proposition twice returns the original proposition.

questions.q: On the Island of Knights and Knaves, how do the two types of inhabitants behave?
o: Knights always lie; knaves always tell the truth
Knights always tell the truth; knaves always lie
questions.e: On the Island of Knights and Knaves, knights always speak the truth and knaves always tell a lie; such puzzles are solved using propositional logic.

questions.q: In a multiple-choice logic problem where the correct answer must be the only correct one, which connective captures 'exactly one is true'?
questions.e: To have only one answer correct — exactly one true — the exclusive OR (XOR) connective is required, since it is true when precisely one of its operands is true.

questions.q: What limitation of propositional logic does predicate logic overcome?
o: Propositional logic cannot represent true or false values
Propositional logic is not expressive enough to deal with quantified variables
Propositional logic cannot use the AND connective
Propositional logic cannot be written symbolically
questions.e: Propositional logic is not expressive enough to deal with quantified variables; predicate logic extends it by adding predicates and quantifiers to capture such statements.

questions.q: What is a predicate?
o: A statement that is always true
A statement that contains variables and may be true or false depending on the values of those variables
questions.e: A predicate is a statement that contains variables (predicate variables) and that may be true or false depending on the values of these variables; for example 'x is greater than 3'.

questions.q: In the statement 'x is greater than 3', which part is the predicate?
o: 'is greater than 3', the property the subject can have
The whole statement is the subject
questions.e: In 'x is greater than 3', the variable x is the subject and 'is greater than 3' is the predicate — it refers to a property that the subject can have.

questions.q: What is the 'universe of discourse' (domain)?
o: The set of all true propositions
The set of all objects that we can sensibly assign to a variable; its elements are called individuals
The set of all logical connectives
questions.e: The universe of discourse is the set of all things we wish to talk about — all objects we can sensibly assign to a variable in a propositional function; its elements are called individuals.

questions.q: What do quantifiers allow us to express?
o: The truth value of a single proposition
How many objects in the universe of discourse satisfy a given predicate
questions.e: Quantifiers provide a notation for quantifying (counting) how many objects in the universe of discourse satisfy a given predicate; quantification binds a variable to a set of values, converting a propositional function into a proposition.

questions.q: What are the two types of quantification?
questions.e: The two types of quantification are universal quantification ('for all' / 'given any') and existential quantification ('there exists').

questions.q: Universal quantification asserts that a property is true in what way?
o: For at least one value of the variable
For all the values of the variable in the domain
questions.e: A universal quantification asserts that a property is true for all the values of a variable in the domain; it means 'given any' or 'for all'.

questions.q: Existential quantification asserts what about a property?
o: It holds for every value in the domain
It holds for at least one value (there exists a value) in the domain
It holds for exactly all but one value
questions.e: Existential quantification asserts that there exists at least one value in the domain for which the predicate holds.

questions.q: What does the negation of a universal quantification become?
questions.e: The negation of a universal quantification becomes an existential quantification, and the negation of an existential quantification becomes a universal quantification.

questions.q: What does the negation of an existential quantification become?
questions.e: The negation of an existential quantification becomes a universal quantification (and vice versa).

questions.q: The statement 'Some snowflakes are the same' has which negation?
o: 'No snowflakes are the same' (equivalently, 'All snowflakes are different')
questions.e: Negating the existential 'Some snowflakes are the same' gives the universal 'No snowflakes are the same', which is equivalent to 'All snowflakes are different'.

questions.q: The 'method of exhaustion' for determining the truth value of a quantified statement means what?
o: If the domain contains a small number of elements, try them all
questions.e: The method of exhaustion says that if the domain contains a small number of elements, you can try them all to determine the truth value of a quantified statement.

questions.q: A conditional statement has three related forms. What are they?
questions.e: A conditional statement has a contrapositive, a converse and an inverse; these definitions can be extended to universal conditional statements.

questions.q: Predicate logic is described as what, relative to propositional logic?
o: An extension of propositional logic that adds predicates and quantifiers
questions.e: Predicate logic is an extension of propositional logic; it adds the concepts of predicates and quantifiers to better capture the meaning of statements that propositional logic cannot adequately express.

questions.q: Statements used in a proof can include which of the following?
o: Axioms (assumed true), premises, and previously proved theorems
questions.e: Statements in a proof can include axioms (something assumed to be true), premises, and previously proved theorems.

questions.q: What are the three main proof techniques?
o: Direct proof, indirect proof, and proof by mathematical induction
Truth tables, Venn diagrams and flowcharts
questions.e: The three proof techniques are direct proof, indirect proof, and proof by mathematical induction; indirect proof itself includes proof by contrapositive and proof by contradiction.

questions.q: How does a direct proof proceed?
o: By assuming the conclusion is false
By starting from the given premises and applying logical deductions based on definitions, theorems and rules of inference to reach the conclusion
questions.e: A direct proof starts with the premises or assumptions known to be true, applies logical deductions based on definitions, theorems and rules of inference, and reaches the conclusion that directly follows.

questions.q: In a direct proof that the product of two odd integers is odd, the integers are written as x = 2n+1 and y = 2m+1. The product simplifies to which form?
o: 2a + 1 (an odd number), where a = 2mn + m + n
questions.e: Writing x = 2n+1 and y = 2m+1 gives xy = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1 = 2a + 1, which is odd, proving the product of two odd integers is odd.

questions.q: In a direct proof that the sum of two odd numbers is even, x = 2n+1 and y = 2m+1 give x + y equal to which form?
questions.e: x + y = (2n+1) + (2m+1) = 2n + 2m + 2 = 2(n + m + 1) = 2a, which is even, proving the sum of two odd numbers is even.

questions.q: What are the two techniques of indirect proof?
o: Proof by contrapositive and proof by contradiction
Proof by exhaustion and proof by cases
questions.e: The two techniques of indirect proof are proof by contrapositive and proof by contradiction.

questions.q: Proof by contrapositive relies on which logical equivalence?
o: p ⇒ q is equivalent to q ⇒ p
p ⇒ q is logically equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q ⇒ ¬p
p ⇒ q is equivalent to p ∧ q
p ⇒ q is equivalent to ¬p ⇒ q
questions.e: Proof by contrapositive uses the fact that p ⇒ q is logically equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q ⇒ ¬p, so proving the contrapositive proves the original.

questions.q: How does proof by contradiction work?
o: Assume q is true and derive q
Assume q is false (its negation true), then by logical argument arrive at a contradiction, which forces q to be true
Try all possible values of q
questions.e: In proof by contradiction, you assume that q is false (its negation is true), then by logical argument arrive at a contradiction; since that can only happen if the negation of q is false, q must be true.

questions.q: Proof by mathematical induction is used to prove a statement true for what?
o: Every natural number (propositions of the form 'for all n, P(n)')
questions.e: Mathematical induction proves that a statement, formula or theorem is true for every natural number, i.e. propositions of the form ∀n P(n).

questions.q: What are the two steps of a proof by mathematical induction?
o: The basis step (show P(1) is true for the initial value) and the inductive step (assume P(k) is true and prove P(k+1))
The forward step and the backward step
The precondition step and the postcondition step
questions.e: A proof by induction has a basis step, which proves the statement true for the initial value (showing P(1) is true), and an inductive step, in which you assume P(k) is true and prove that P(k+1) is then true.

questions.q: In the inductive step of mathematical induction, what is assumed and what must be proved?
o: Assume P(k) is true; prove that P(k+1) is true
questions.e: In the inductive step you assume that P(k) is true (the inductive hypothesis) and must then prove that P(k+1) is also true.

questions.q: The basis step of mathematical induction typically proves the statement true for which value?
questions.e: The basis step proves that the statement is true for the initial value (the basic value, usually assumed to be 1); that is, it shows that P(1) is true.

questions.q: A direct proof of a statement of the form 'if p then q' begins from what?
o: The premises or assumptions that are given or known to be true
questions.e: A direct proof starts with the premises or assumptions that are given or known to be true and applies logical deductions to reach the conclusion.

questions.q: Why might proving the contrapositive be easier than proving 'if p then q' directly?
o: Because the contrapositive is a different statement with a different truth value
Because the contrapositive ¬q ⇒ ¬p is logically equivalent, so proving it proves the original, and it can be a more convenient starting point
Because the contrapositive is always true
Because the contrapositive removes the need for premises
questions.e: Since p ⇒ q is logically equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q ⇒ ¬p, proving the contrapositive establishes the original statement, and starting from ¬q can sometimes lead more directly to ¬p.

questions.q: What is the Cartesian product A × B of two sets A and B?
o: The set of elements common to A and B
The set of all ordered pairs (a, b) where a ∈ A and b ∈ B
The set of elements in A but not B
The union of A and B
questions.e: The Cartesian product A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) where a ∈ A and b ∈ B, written A × B = {(a, b) | a ∈ A and b ∈ B}.

questions.q: A binary relation R from set A to set B is defined as what?
o: A function from A to B
A set of ordered pairs where the first element is from A and the second from B, i.e. R ⊆ A × B
The Cartesian product A × B itself only
questions.e: A binary relation from A to B is a set of ordered pairs whose first element is from A and second from B; formally R is a relation from A to B if R ⊆ A × B. Every relation is a subset of a Cartesian product.

questions.q: The domain of a relation R from A to B is which set?
o: The set of all second elements of the ordered pairs in R
The set of all first elements of the ordered pairs which belong to R
questions.e: The domain Dom(R) is the set of all first elements of the ordered pairs belonging to R: Dom(R) = {a ∈ A | (a,b) ∈ R}. The range is the set of all second elements.

questions.q: The range of a relation R from A to B is which set?
o: The set of all first elements of the ordered pairs in R
The set of all second elements of the ordered pairs which belong to R
questions.e: The range Ran(R) is the set of all second elements of the ordered pairs belonging to R: Ran(R) = {b ∈ B | (a,b) ∈ R}.

questions.q: A relation R on a set A is reflexive if which condition holds?
o: (a, a) ∉ R for all a ∈ A
(a, a) ∈ R for all a ∈ A (every element is related to itself)
(a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R implies (a, c) ∈ R
questions.e: A relation R on A is reflexive if (a, a) ∈ R for all a ∈ A, meaning every element is related to itself. Every identity relation is reflexive, but not every reflexive relation is an identity relation.

questions.q: A relation R is symmetric if which condition holds?
o: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, a) ∈ R implies a = b
(a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R implies (a, c) ∈ R
questions.e: A relation R is symmetric if and only if whenever (a, b) ∈ R then (b, a) ∈ R as well (aRb implies bRa).

questions.q: A relation R on A is antisymmetric if which condition holds?
o: whenever (a, b) ∈ R and (b, a) ∈ R, then a = b
(a, b) ∉ R for all a, b
questions.e: A relation R on A is antisymmetric if whenever both (a, b) ∈ R and (b, a) ∈ R, then a = b (i.e. (a,b) ∈ R with a ≠ b forces (b,a) ∉ R).

questions.q: A relation R on A is transitive if which condition holds?
o: if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R then (a, c) ∈ R
questions.e: A relation R is transitive if and only if for all a, b, c: if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R then (a, c) ∈ R (if aRb and bRc then aRc).

questions.q: The empty relation and the full relation between sets X and Y are respectively which sets?
o: The full relation is ∅; the empty relation is X × Y
The empty relation is ∅; the full relation is X × Y
questions.e: The empty relation between X and Y is the empty set ∅, while the full relation is the entire Cartesian product X × Y.

questions.q: What is a function from set A to set B?
o: A relation in which each and every element of A has a unique image in B
A relation where some elements of A have no image
A relation where an element of A can map to several elements of B
questions.e: A function is a rule or mapping from A to B such that each and every element of A has a unique image in B; formally, for every a ∈ A there is a unique b ∈ B with (a, b) ∈ f.

questions.q: For a relation to define a function from X to Y, which two conditions must hold?
o: Every element of Y must be used, and pairs may repeat first elements
Every element of X must be the first element of some pair, and no two pairs have the same first element with different second elements
The relation must be symmetric and transitive
The relation must be empty or full
questions.e: A relation defines a function if every element of X appears as the first element of some ordered pair, and there is no pair with the same first element but a different second element (each input has exactly one output).

questions.q: When is a function f injective (one-to-one)?
o: When every element of Y is an image of some x
When distinct elements of the domain map to distinct elements of the codomain (x1 ≠ x2 implies f(x1) ≠ f(x2))
When f maps everything to a single value
When f is both onto and reflexive
questions.e: A function f is injective (one-to-one) if and only if for all x1, x2, whenever x1 ≠ x2 then f(x1) ≠ f(x2); distinct elements must have distinct images.

questions.q: When is a function f surjective (onto)?
o: When distinct inputs give distinct outputs
When each element of the codomain Y equals f(x) for some x in the domain
When it maps to at most one element
questions.e: A function f is surjective (onto) if each element of Y equals g(x) for some x in X — that is, every element of the codomain is hit by some input.

questions.q: A bijective function (one-to-one correspondence) is one that is what?
questions.e: A bijective function, or one-to-one correspondence, is a function that is both one-to-one (injective) and onto (surjective).

questions.q: How many one-to-one functions exist from a set with three elements to a set with two elements?
questions.e: There is no one-to-one function from a set with three elements to a set with two elements, because after mapping two elements to the two available images, there is no new image left for the third element.

questions.q: Given A = {1, 2}, B = {1, 2, 3} and R = {(a,b) ∈ A × B | a < b}, what are the ordered pairs in R?
questions.e: The pairs with a < b are (1,2), (1,3) and (2,3), so R = {(1,2), (1,3), (2,3)}, with Dom(R) = {1,2} and Ran(R) = {2,3}.

questions.q: An ordered pair (a, b) differs from a set {a, b} in what way?
o: An ordered pair cannot contain numbers
In an ordered pair the order matters (a is the first element and b the second), whereas in a set order is not significant
An ordered pair may contain only one element
questions.e: An ordered pair (a, b) consists of a first element a and a second element b in a specific order, whereas a set is an unordered collection; relations are built from ordered pairs.

questions.q: The inverse of a surjective function has which noted property?
o: It is always a bijective function
It may not be a function
questions.e: The inverse of a surjective function may not be a function, because a surjection can map several inputs to the same output, so reversing it can give one input several images.

questions.q: A relation R is called a relation 'on' a set A when?
o: R ⊆ A × B for a different set B
R ⊆ A × A (both elements of each pair come from A)
questions.e: When R ⊆ A × A — that is, both the first and second elements of every pair come from the same set A — R is called a relation on A.

questions.q: What is a sequence?
o: A set of distinct unordered objects
A list, such as 2, 4, 6, ..., in which the numbers are the terms of the sequence
questions.e: A sequence is simply a list, such as 2, 4, 6, ..., where the numbers are the terms of the sequence; terms are indexed by n and the sequence value for a specific term is often written a_n.

questions.q: What is the difference between a finite and an infinite sequence?
o: A finite sequence has no starting value; an infinite one does
A finite sequence has both a starting and an ending value; an infinite sequence has a starting value but no ending value
A finite sequence cannot contain numbers
questions.e: A finite sequence has both a starting value and an ending value (e.g. 1,2,3,4,5,6), whereas an infinite sequence has a starting value but no ending value (e.g. 1,2,3,4,5,6,...).

questions.q: What defines an arithmetic sequence?
o: Each term is obtained by multiplying or dividing by the same value
Each term is obtained from the previous one by always adding or subtracting the same value
Each term is the sum of the two previous terms
Each term is the square of the previous term
questions.e: An arithmetic sequence goes from one term to the next by always adding or subtracting the same value, called the common difference (d).

questions.q: What defines a geometric sequence?
o: Each term is obtained by adding the same value
Each term is obtained from the previous one by always multiplying or dividing by the same value
Each term is a prime number
Each term equals the term index
questions.e: A geometric sequence goes from one term to the next by always multiplying or dividing by the same value (the common ratio).

questions.q: In the arithmetic sequence -9, -2, 5, ..., what is the common difference d?
questions.e: The common difference is what you add to get the next term: -2 - (-9) = 7 and 5 - (-2) = 7, so d = 7 and the next terms are 12, 19, 26, 33.

questions.q: What is the common difference of the arithmetic sequence 0, 7, 14, ...?
questions.e: Each term increases by 7 (7 - 0 = 7, 14 - 7 = 7), so the common difference d = 7 and the next terms are 21, 28, 35, 42.

questions.q: For the arithmetic sequence 5k, -k, -7k, ..., what is the common difference?
questions.e: The common difference is -k - 5k = -6k (and -7k - (-k) = -6k), so d = -6k and the following terms are -13k, -19k, -25k.

questions.q: What is the nth partial sum of a sequence?
o: The nth term of the sequence
The sum of the first n terms of the sequence
The product of the first n terms
The average of all the terms
questions.e: The nth partial sum is the sum of the first n terms of an (infinite) sequence.

questions.q: The two arithmetic means between -4 and 5 are which values?
questions.e: Inserting two arithmetic means gives -4, -1, 2, 5, an arithmetic sequence with common difference 3, so the two arithmetic means are -1 and 2.

questions.q: The two geometric means between -2 and 54 are which values?
questions.e: Inserting two geometric means gives -2, 6, -18, 54, a geometric sequence (ratio -3), so the two geometric means are 6 and -18.

questions.q: In sigma (summation) notation, what do the numbers written above and below the sigma symbol represent?
o: The first and last terms of the sequence
The upper bound and the lower bound of the summation index
The common difference and common ratio
questions.e: In sigma notation, the number below the sigma is the lower bound and the number above is the upper bound of the summation index, while the expression to the right is the nth term (the sequence being summed).

questions.q: To what does the index n (the term number) of a sequence typically refer?
o: The value of a specific term
The position or index of a term, running from 0 to infinity
questions.e: The term index (usually written with the subscript n) refers to the position of a term in the sequence, starting from 0 and running to infinity, whereas a (a specific letter) refers to the value at that term.

questions.q: How is a set defined?
o: An ordered list that may contain duplicates
An unordered collection of distinct objects (its elements or members)
A sequence of numbers with a common difference
A mapping from one set to another
questions.e: A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects, which are called its elements or members; sets do not contain duplicates and the order of elements is not significant.

questions.q: In set notation, what does the double-equals symbol (==) mean, as in Vowels == {a,e,i,o,u}?
questions.e: The double-equals symbol (==) is read 'is defined to be'; it provides a method for naming sets so they can be reused, e.g. Vowels == {a,e,i,o,u}.

questions.q: Which pre-defined set is denoted N and defined as the natural numbers?
questions.e: In this notation N denotes the natural numbers {1,2,3,...}; N1 denotes the naturals greater than 1 ({2,3,...}), Z the integers {...,-2,-1,0,1,2,...}, and B the truth values {true, false}.

questions.q: Which set is denoted B and what are its members?
questions.e: B denotes the set of truth values, B = {true, false}. Z denotes the integers and N the natural numbers.

questions.q: What does the cardinality of a set measure, and how is it denoted?
o: The largest element, denoted with braces
The number of elements in the set, denoted with vertical bars, e.g. |{1,3,9,15}| = 4
questions.e: Cardinality is the number of elements in a set, denoted by vertical bars around the set; for example |{1, 3, 9, 15}| = 4 and |{1, 2, 3, ...}| = ∞.

questions.q: Two sets A and B are disjoint when?
o: They contain exactly the same members
Every member of A has no relation with B and vice versa (they share no members)
A is a subset of B
questions.e: Sets A and B are disjoint if every member of A has no relation with B and vice versa — that is, they have no members in common.

questions.q: For A = {-1, 0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 10} and B = {1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10}, what is the set difference A - B?
questions.e: The difference A - B contains the elements found in A but not in B: {-1, 0, 5, 9}. (By contrast B - A = {4, 8}.)

questions.q: The subset relation S ⊆ T is true when?
o: S and T have no members in common
Every member of S is also a member of T
S has more members than T
S equals the empty set only
questions.e: S ⊆ T is true if every member of S is also a member of T; for example {1,2,3} ⊆ N and N ⊆ Z.

questions.q: What is a proper subset of a set A?
o: Any subset of A, including A itself
A subset of A that is not equal to A (A contains at least one element not in the subset)
questions.e: A proper subset of A is a subset of A that is not equal to A; all its elements are in A, but A contains at least one element not in the proper subset.

questions.q: What is a key property of the empty set ∅?
o: It has no members, so x ∈ ∅ is false for any value x
It is a subset of no set
questions.e: The empty set ∅ (also written {}) has no members, so for any value x the expression x ∈ ∅ is false.

questions.q: The power set P(S) of a set S is which set?
o: The set of all members of S
The set of all subsets of S
The set S with one element removed
questions.e: The power set P(S) is the set of all subsets of S. For example, if S = {1,2} then P(S) = {∅, {1}, {2}, {1,2}}.

questions.q: If S = {1, 2}, what is its power set P(S)?
questions.e: The power set of {1,2} is the set of all its subsets: {∅, {1}, {2}, {1,2}}, which has 4 = 2^2 elements.

questions.q: The union A ∪ B contains which elements?
o: Only elements in both A and B
All elements contained in either set (x ∈ A or x ∈ B, or both)
Elements in A but not B
questions.e: The union A ∪ B contains all elements contained in either set or both: x ∈ A ∪ B if x ∈ A or x ∈ B (or both).

questions.q: The intersection A ∩ B contains which elements?
o: Only the elements that are in both sets (x ∈ A and x ∈ B)
Elements in A but not B
questions.e: The intersection A ∩ B contains only the elements that are in both sets: x ∈ A ∩ B if x ∈ A and x ∈ B.

questions.q: The complement of a set A contains what?
o: Everything that is not in A (equivalently, the universal set minus A)
The elements common to A and the universal set
questions.e: The complement of A (written A', A^c or ~A) contains everything that is not in the set A; it equals the difference between the universal set and A.

questions.q: For H = {cat, dog, rabbit, mouse} and F = {dog, cow, duck, pig, rabbit}, what is H ∩ F?
o: {cat, dog, rabbit, mouse, cow, duck, pig}
questions.e: The intersection H ∩ F contains the elements common to both sets: {dog, rabbit}.

questions.q: Why is the expression {1,2,3} ∈ {4,5,6} not allowed, while {1,2,3} ∈ {{6,7,8},{1,2,3}} is allowed?
o: Because the right-hand side of x ∈ S must be a set whose members are of the same type as x; {4,5,6} contains numbers, not sets, whereas the second set contains sets
Because ∈ can only be used with the empty set
Because {1,2,3} is not a valid set
questions.e: In x ∈ S the right-hand side must return a set of values of the same type as x. {1,2,3} is a set of numbers, so it can be a member of a set of sets like {{6,7,8},{1,2,3}} (true), but not of a set of numbers like {4,5,6}.

questions.q: Set equality {1,2,3} = {2,3,1} is true because of which property of sets?
o: The order in which values occur in a set is not significant
questions.e: Two sets of the same type are equal if they contain precisely the same members; since the order of elements in a set is not significant, {1,2,3} = {2,3,1} is true.

questions.q: What is Hoare logic, and who proposed it?
o: A programming language proposed by Dijkstra in 1975
A formal system of logical rules for reasoning rigorously about the correctness of computer programs, proposed by Tony Hoare in 1969
A testing framework proposed by Turing
questions.e: Hoare logic (also Floyd-Hoare logic or Hoare rules) is a formal system with logical rules for reasoning rigorously about program correctness; it was proposed in 1969 by the British computer scientist Tony Hoare.

questions.q: Hoare logic treats a specification as a contract made up of which two parts?
questions.e: Hoare logic is based on the idea of a specification as a contract between a function's implementation and its clients, made up of a precondition and a postcondition.

questions.q: What is a precondition in Hoare logic?
o: A predicate the function establishes after running
A predicate describing the condition the function relies on for correct operation, which the client must fulfil
The final state of the program
questions.e: The precondition is a predicate describing the condition the function relies on for correct operation; the client must fulfil this condition before calling the function.

questions.q: What is a postcondition in Hoare logic?
o: A condition the client must satisfy before calling
A predicate describing the condition the function establishes after correctly running, which the client can rely on afterward
questions.e: The postcondition is a predicate describing the condition the function establishes after correctly running; the client can rely on it being true after the call.

questions.q: In Hoare logic, what is a 'state'?
o: An association between program variables and their values
The result returned by a function
questions.e: A state is an association between program variables and their values.

questions.q: A program is 'partially correct' with respect to its specification if what holds?
o: Assuming the precondition is true before execution, then IF the function terminates, the postcondition is true
The postcondition is true even if the precondition is false
questions.e: Partial correctness means that, assuming the precondition holds just before execution, then if the function terminates, the postcondition is true — termination is not guaranteed.

questions.q: How does total correctness relate to partial correctness?
o: Total correctness is weaker than partial correctness
Total correctness is partial correctness plus termination (the function is guaranteed to terminate and then the postcondition holds)
questions.e: Total correctness is partial correctness plus termination: assuming the precondition holds, the function is guaranteed to terminate, and when it does the postcondition is true.

questions.q: A Hoare triple {P} C {Q} expresses what?
o: That P, C and Q are all equal
That when the precondition P is met, executing the command C establishes the postcondition Q
That C is executed before P
That Q is the negation of P
questions.e: A Hoare triple {P} C {Q} has assertions P (precondition) and Q (postcondition) and a command C; it states that when the precondition P is met, executing the command C establishes the postcondition Q.

questions.q: When is a Hoare triple invalid?
o: When there is a scenario in which the precondition P is true, the command executes, and the postcondition Q is false afterward
Whenever the command changes a variable
When P and Q are the same
questions.e: A Hoare triple is invalid if there can be a scenario where P is true, the statement executes, and Q is false afterward. If P is false, the triple promises nothing about Q.

questions.q: What is an assertion in the context of reasoning about code?
o: A logical formula inserted at some point in a program, presumed to hold true at that point
questions.e: An assertion is a logical formula inserted at some point in a program that is presumed to hold true at that point; the special assertions are the precondition (before execution) and postcondition (after).

questions.q: What is the difference between forward reasoning and backward reasoning about code?
o: Forward reasoning starts from the postcondition; backward from the precondition
Forward reasoning simulates execution in statement order (and may accumulate irrelevant facts); backward reasoning pushes the postcondition up through the statements to find the precondition
Forward reasoning ignores the precondition; backward ignores the postcondition
They always give different final results
questions.e: Forward reasoning simulates execution, considering statements in the order they execute, and can accumulate many irrelevant facts. Backward reasoning starts from the desired postcondition and pushes it up through the statements to determine the required precondition; it is often more useful.

questions.q: What is the weakest precondition of a command C for a postcondition Q?
o: The most restrictive precondition that guarantees Q
The most general (least restrictive) precondition needed to establish the postcondition Q
A precondition that is always false
questions.e: The weakest precondition is the most general (least restrictive) precondition needed to establish the postcondition; a weaker assertion is more general, a stronger one more specific. It is written P = wp(S, Q).

questions.q: The assignment rule states that wp(x = e, Q) equals what?
o: Q with all free occurrences of e replaced by x
Q with all free occurrences of x replaced by e
questions.e: The weakest precondition of an assignment is wp(x = e, Q) = Q with all free occurrences of x replaced by e; for example wp(x = y+1, x > 0) = (y+1 > 0).

questions.q: Using the assignment rule, what is wp(x = y+1, x > 0)?
questions.e: Substituting y+1 for x in the postcondition x > 0 gives the weakest precondition y+1 > 0.

questions.q: For a statement list S1; S2, how is the weakest precondition computed?
o: wp(S1; S2, Q) = wp(S1, Q) and wp(S2, Q) independently
wp(S1; S2, Q) = wp(S1, wp(S2, Q))
wp(S1; S2, Q) = wp(S2, wp(S1, Q))
questions.e: For consecutive statements, the weakest precondition is found by working backwards: wp(S1; S2, Q) = wp(S1, wp(S2, Q)); first find X = wp(S2, Q), then wp(S1, X).

questions.q: What is the weakest precondition of the assignment n := n - 1 for the postcondition n < 0?
questions.e: Substituting n-1 for n in n < 0 gives n-1 < 0, i.e. n <= 0, so wp(n := n-1, n < 0) = (n <= 0).

questions.q: What is a loop invariant?
o: A variable that never changes value
An assertion that is both a precondition and postcondition for the loop body, true at the beginning and end of each iteration
The condition that ends the loop
The initial value of the loop counter
questions.e: A loop invariant {I} is a precondition and postcondition for the loop body; it must be true at the beginning and end of each iteration (though not necessarily at every point in the middle).

questions.q: To prove a postcondition Q holds after a loop with invariant I and condition B, one shows I holds before the loop, I is preserved by the body, and which final condition?
questions.e: After showing I holds before the loop and is preserved by each iteration, the final step is to show that {I ∧ ¬B} → {Q}: when the loop exits (B is false) with the invariant still true, the postcondition Q must follow.

questions.q: The assignment rule for finding a precondition can be described informally as which of the following?
o: Delete the variable from the postcondition
Take the postcondition and replace the variable with the value assigned on the right-hand side of the statement
Add the assigned value to the postcondition
questions.e: Informally, the assignment rule says: take the postcondition and replace the variable in it with the value assigned on the right-hand side of the assignment statement.

questions.q: What kind of language is Z?
o: A programming language that can be compiled and executed
A strongly typed, mathematical specification language that is neither a natural nor a programming language and cannot be executed
A natural language for writing requirements
questions.e: Z is neither a natural language nor a programming language but a combination of characteristics of both; it is a strongly typed, mathematical specification language that cannot be executed, interpreted or compiled into a running program.

questions.q: Who originally proposed Z and where was it further developed?
o: Jean-Raymond Abrial, Steve Schuman and Bertrand Meyer in 1977, further developed at Oxford University
Krysta Yousoufian, at the University of Washington
questions.e: Z was proposed by Jean-Raymond Abrial, Steve Schuman and Bertrand Meyer in 1977 and was later further developed at the Programming Research Group at Oxford University.

questions.q: What is the basic unit of specification in Z?
questions.e: The basic unit of specification in Z is a schema; Z allows a specification to be decomposed into small pieces called schemas.

questions.q: A Z schema consists of which three components?
o: A unique name, a signature (declaring entities and their types), and a predicate part (defining invariants)
questions.e: A Z schema consists of a unique name/identifier, a signature that declares entities and their types (variable declarations), and a predicate part that defines invariants involving those entities.

questions.q: In the box-like structure of a Z schema, where are declarations and predicates written?
o: Declarations below the central line, predicates above
Declarations above the central line, predicates below it
questions.e: In a Z schema, all declarations are made above the central line and the predicates are defined below the central line.

questions.q: What is the difference between the static and dynamic aspects of a system in Z?
o: Static aspects are the operations; dynamic aspects are the invariants
Static aspects are the states the system can occupy and the invariants maintained; dynamic aspects are the operations, their inputs/outputs and the state changes
Static aspects concern speed; dynamic aspects concern memory
questions.e: Static aspects are the states a system can occupy and the invariant relationships maintained across states; dynamic aspects are the operations that are possible, the relationship between their inputs and outputs, and the changes of state.

questions.q: In Z, what do the identifier suffixes ?, ! and ' (prime) denote?
o: ? = input variable, ! = output variable, ' = new value after a state change
questions.e: In Z, an identifier suffixed with ? is an input variable, one suffixed with ! is an output variable, and one suffixed with ' (prime) denotes the new value of a variable following a state change.

questions.q: Which types are built into Z?
o: The integers Z, the natural numbers N (0,1,2,...) and the positive integers N1; the reals are NOT built in
questions.e: Z's built-in types include the integers (Z), the natural numbers N = {0,1,2,...} and the positive integers N1; the reals are not a built-in type. Free types are similar to enumerated types in C++.

questions.q: In Z, what does the operator # denote?
o: The cardinality of a finite set
questions.e: In Z the operator # denotes the cardinality of a finite set.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a Delta (Δ) schema in Z?
o: To specify an operation that does not change the state
To create a new schema combining the before and after specifications of a state, for operations that change the state
questions.e: The Delta (Δ) prefix creates a new schema by combining the before and after specifications of a state; it is used for operations that change the state of a structure.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a Xi (Ξ) schema in Z?
o: To specify operations that change the state
To specify operations (such as inquiries) that do NOT change the state of a structure
questions.e: The Xi (Ξ) prefix, like Delta, is obtained by combining the before and after specifications of a state, but it is used to specify operations (such as inquiries) that do not change the state.

questions.q: Model-based specification languages such as Z describe a system in what way?
o: As a set of algebraic axioms about operations
As a system state model built from mathematical entities (sets, relations, sequences, functions), with operations specified by their effect on the state via pre and post conditions
As a flowchart of control flow
questions.e: In a model-based language the specification is expressed as a system state model built from sets, relations, sequences and functions; operations are specified by how they affect the state, described by predicates given as pre and post conditions.

questions.q: The Z notation is composed of which two sub-languages?
o: A syntax language and a semantics language
A mathematical language (propositional and predicate logic, sets, relations, functions) and a schema language (for structuring and composing descriptions)
An input language and an output language
A static language and a dynamic language
questions.e: Z has a mathematical language, used to describe objects and their relationships (propositional logic, predicate logic, sets, relations, functions), and a schema language, used to structure and compose descriptions by collecting, encapsulating and naming pieces for reuse.

questions.q: What does schema calculus enable in Z?
o: Building large schemas from smaller ones (e.g. separating normal operations from error handling), achieving separation of concerns
Removing all predicates from a schema
questions.e: Schema calculus modularises specifications by building large schemas from smaller ones — for example separating normal operations from error handling — achieving separation of concerns; conjunction and disjunction are the most useful operators.

questions.q: Why is formal specification particularly important for mission- and safety-critical systems?
o: Because such systems have simple requirements
Because failure can cause cost overruns, loss of lives or severe economic consequences, so errors must be uncovered before the software is put into operation
Because they do not need testing
Because they cannot be modelled mathematically
questions.e: In mission- and safety-critical systems, failure can cause cost overruns, loss of lives or severe economic consequences, so it is necessary that errors are uncovered before the software is put into operation.

questions.q: According to the definition given, a formal specification describes what, rather than how?
o: How the system is implemented in code
What the system should do, not necessarily how it should do it
How much memory the system uses
questions.e: A formal specification is a mathematical description of software or hardware that describes what the system should do, not necessarily how the system should do it; formal verification can then show a candidate design is correct with respect to it.

questions.q: In the BirthdayBook Z specification, the state has known: P NAME and birthday: NAME ↦ DATE. What is the state invariant?
o: known = dom birthday (known is the set of names for which birthday is defined)
questions.e: The BirthdayBook invariant is known = dom birthday: the set known is exactly the domain of the function birthday — the set of names to which the birthday function can validly be applied.

questions.q: In the BirthdayBook specification, what does 'birthday' represent?
o: A function which, when applied to a name, gives the birthday (date) associated with it
questions.e: birthday is a function which, when applied to a name, gives the birthday associated with it; because it is a function, each person can have only one birthday.

questions.q: The state invariant known = dom birthday is described as being true when?
o: In every state of the system, maintained by every operation on it
Only when the book is empty
questions.e: The relationship known = dom birthday is an invariant of the system: it is true in every state of the system and is maintained by every operation on it.

questions.q: The AddBirthday operation includes ΔBirthdayBook, inputs name? and date?, the precondition name? ∉ known, and which effect?
questions.e: AddBirthday changes state (ΔBirthdayBook), requires that name? is not already known (name? ∉ known), and extends the birthday function: birthday' = birthday ∪ {name? ↦ date?}.

questions.q: Why does the FindBirthday operation include ΞBirthdayBook rather than ΔBirthdayBook?
o: Because it adds a new entry
Because finding a birthday does not change the state of the database
questions.e: FindBirthday includes ΞBirthdayBook because it is a query that does not change the state; it takes name? ∈ known and outputs date! = birthday(name?).

questions.q: The Remind operation outputs cards! = {n : known | birthday(n) = today?}. What does this set contain?
o: All dates in the birthday function
The set of all names n drawn from known whose birthday equals the given date today?
The single name with the earliest birthday
questions.e: Remind (a Ξ operation, state unchanged) outputs cards!, the set of all names n from known such that birthday(n) = today? — everyone whose birthday is the given date.

questions.q: The InitBirthdayBook operation specifies what?
o: known = ∅ (the birthday book is initially empty)
questions.e: InitBirthdayBook creates the birthday book in its initial state with known = ∅ — the birthday book is initially empty.

questions.q: The RAddBirthday (robust add) schema is defined as (AddBirthday ∧ Success) ∨ AlreadyKnown. What does the AlreadyKnown schema handle?
o: Adding a birthday for a new person
The error case where name? ∈ known, producing the report 'Already known'
questions.e: AlreadyKnown handles the error case: it is a Ξ operation with name? ∈ known and result! = Already known; RAddBirthday combines the successful AddBirthday (with Success) and this error case using disjunction.

questions.q: How is the robust operation RAddBirthday built from simpler schemas?
o: By using Z schema calculus to combine AddBirthday, Success and AlreadyKnown: (AddBirthday ∧ Success) ∨ AlreadyKnown
questions.e: RAddBirthday is a new schema obtained with schema calculus by combining three already-defined schemas: (AddBirthday ∧ Success) ∨ AlreadyKnown, so it behaves correctly for valid input and reports an error otherwise.

questions.q: The Success schema outputs result! = ok. Why is it combined (by conjunction) with AddBirthday?
o: To provide an indication that the add operation was successful, giving a total operation that both adds and reports 'ok' for correct input
questions.e: The Success schema just produces the report ok; combining it by conjunction with AddBirthday (AddBirthday ∧ Success) describes an operation that, for correct input, both adds the birthday and reports success.

questions.q: In the insulin pump Z schema, the safety constraint on doses states which limits?
o: A single dose may be up to 50 units and total dose up to 5 units
No single dose may exceed 5 units of insulin, and the total (cumulative) dose in a time period must not exceed 50 units
The dose must always equal the capacity
There is no limit on the dose
questions.e: The insulin pump's safety invariant requires that no single dose is more than 5 units of insulin and the cumulative dose delivered in a time period must not exceed 50 units; the dose must also be at most the reservoir capacity.

questions.q: In the insulin pump schema, what does the invariant part of a Z schema define?
o: The operations that change the state
Conditions that are always true (for example the dose and cumulative-dose safety limits)
The input and output variables only
The initial state of the pump
questions.e: Each Z schema has an invariant part that defines conditions that are always true; for the insulin pump it is always true, for example, that the dose is at most the capacity and within the safety limits.

questions.q: The Birthday Book study notes that the INSULIN_PUMP and DISPLAY schemas are inconsistent because display1! is used for two different purposes. Why does this matter?
o: Inconsistency makes the specification run faster
Inconsistency suggests a problem with the system requirements that must be resolved before implementation
It has no effect on the system
questions.e: In one schema display1! shows a warning about the insulin reservoir and in another it shows the blood-sugar state; this inconsistency suggests a problem with the requirements and must be resolved before the system is implemented.

questions.q: In the BirthdayBook, a state might be known = {Ahmed, Iram, Farrukh} with birthday mapping Ahmed ↦ 25-Mar, Iram ↦ 20-Dec, Farrukh ↦ 25-Mar. What does this illustrate about the birthday function?
o: That a name can have two birthdays
That two different names (Ahmed and Farrukh) can map to the same date, but each name still has exactly one birthday
That known can differ from the domain of birthday
questions.e: The state shows that two different people (Ahmed and Farrukh) can share the same date (25-Mar), which is allowed because birthday is a function only in that each name maps to exactly one date; the invariant known = dom birthday still holds.

questions.q: What is an abstract machine?
o: A physical computer used only for testing
A model of a computer system, constructed to allow precise analysis of how it works, usually consisting of input, output and an operation set
A compiler for the B language
questions.e: An abstract machine is a model of a computer system (hardware or software) constructed to allow detailed and precise analysis of how it works; it usually consists of input, output and a set of operations (the operation set), so it can be thought of as a processor.

questions.q: In Abstract Machine Notation, what are the main components of a machine?
o: MACHINE (name), VARIABLES (state), INVARIANT, INITIALIZATION and OPERATIONS
questions.e: An AMN machine has a MACHINE name, VARIABLES that hold the state, an INVARIANT (conditions always true of the state, e.g. types), an INITIALIZATION (initial state), and OPERATIONS.

questions.q: In AMN, the INVARIANT component specifies what?
o: Information that must be true of the state, such as the types of the state variables (which must not change during execution)
questions.e: The INVARIANT lists information that must always be true of the state, including the types of the state variables and other constraints; for example, a variable's type must not change during execution.

questions.q: An AMN machine is compared to which programming-language construct?
o: A class (SIMULA), module (MODULA) or package (ADA) — a well-defined, self-contained unit
questions.e: The notion of an abstract machine is a central feature of AMN and is the specification analogue of what in programming languages is known as a class (SIMULA), a module (MODULA) or a package (ADA); a machine can be pictured as a black box with buttons (operations) and internal state variables.

questions.q: What is the B specification method, and on what is it based?
o: A testing method based on random inputs
The B Abstract Machine Notation specification approach, developed in the 1980s by J.R. Abrial and others, based on sets and first-order logic
A hardware design language based on circuits
questions.e: The B Abstract Machine Notation specification language was originally developed in the early and mid 1980s by J.R. Abrial and research groups at BP Research; B specification is based on sets and first-order logic.

questions.q: In the B-method, what is a 'proof obligation' and why does it matter?
o: A test that must pass before release
A property that must be proved — such as that an operation preserves the invariant — which is key to the correctness of the design
A precondition that is always false
questions.e: Proof obligations are the key to the correctness of a design: it must be proved that the specification of each operation preserves the invariant (assuming the state satisfies the invariant before the operation, the invariant is satisfied after). Other obligations concern the initialisation establishing the invariant and the invariant not being trivially false.

questions.q: In AMN, how is an operation's header written to show its outputs and inputs?
questions.e: In B/AMN an operation header lists the outputs, a left-pointing arrow, then the operation name and inputs: outputs ← name(inputs).

questions.q: In AMN, an operation is often written as a pre-conditioned substitution: 'pre Q then S end'. What does this mean?
o: The substitution S is always performed
The substitution S is only carried out if the formulas Q between 'pre' and 'then' are satisfied; if not, anything might happen
Q is the output of the operation
S is executed before Q is checked
questions.e: An AMN operation defined as 'pre Q then S end' is a pre-conditioned substitution: the substitution S is carried out only if the precondition Q is satisfied; if Q is not satisfied, then anything might happen.

questions.q: One major difference between Z and AMN concerns combining specifications. What is it?
o: Z machines can be combined in many ways; AMN cannot combine at all

In Z a specification can essentially only be combined by concatenation, whereas in AMN an abstract machine is a well-defined unit with several carefully designed ways of combining machines (e.g. uses, includes)
Neither Z nor AMN can combine specifications
questions.e: In Z there is no way of combining two specifications except concatenation, whereas in AMN an abstract machine is a well-defined unit and there are several thought-out ways of combining machines, such as one machine 'using' or 'including' another.

questions.q: A key difference between Z and AMN regarding proof is which of the following?
o: Z requires proof obligations; AMN does not
In the B-method (AMN) certain properties are singled out as proof obligations that must be discharged, whereas in Z ensuring the invariant is preserved is left at the intuitive level
AMN cannot prove anything about specifications
questions.e: In the B-method for AMN, certain properties are singled out as proof obligations; if they are discharged the specifier knows the specification has desirable properties. In Z there is no such obligation, and ensuring the state invariant is preserved is left entirely at the intuitive level.

questions.q: In AMN, how does an operation indicate that a variable is unchanged, compared with Z?
o: AMN must list every unchanged variable, like Z
In Z you must explicitly state that a variable is unchanged (e.g. telephones' = telephones), but in AMN there is no need to mention variables unchanged by an operation
Neither Z nor AMN mentions unchanged variables
questions.e: In Z you must explicitly mention whether a variable is affected (e.g. writing telephones' = telephones to show it does not change), which is tedious for large specifications; in AMN there is no need to mention variables that are unchanged by an operation.

questions.q: How do Z and AMN differ in the treatment of preconditions?
o: AMN hides preconditions; Z states them explicitly
In AMN the preconditions of an operation must be explicitly mentioned, whereas in a Z schema the preconditions are not singled out (though a precondition schema can be calculated)
Both require preconditions to be omitted
questions.e: In AMN the preconditions of an operation must be explicitly mentioned (between 'pre' and 'then'); in a Z schema the preconditions are not singled out in any special way, although it is possible to calculate the precondition schema from an operation schema.

questions.q: In the AMN symbol := used in initialisation (e.g. members, telephones := ∅, ∅), what does it represent, given that Z is model-based while AMN is built on textual substitution?
o: Ordinary assignment as in a programming language
Substitution (not assignment) — here the simultaneous substitution of ∅ for both variables — performed on a description of the system state
questions.e: In AMN the := in the initialisation component is not assignment but substitution; members, telephones := ∅, ∅ is the simultaneous substitution of ∅ for both variables. Whereas Z is a model-based specification language, AMN is built on the idea of textual substitution.

questions.q: In the Internal Telephone Number Database comparison, how many operations does the system provide, and what are examples?
o: Six operations, including adding/removing a person, adding/removing an entry, and interrogating the database by person or by extension
questions.e: The Internal Telephone Number Database provides six operations: adding a person, removing a person, adding an entry (a person-extension association), removing an entry, interrogating by person, and interrogating by extension number.

questions.q: How is a low-level AMN specification related to program code?
o: By manual translation with no formal basis
By means of Dijkstra's weakest-precondition calculus, integrated into the AMN specification-design-implementation process
By compiling the Z schemas directly
By running the abstract machine on hardware
questions.e: In AMN a low-level specification is related to program code by means of Dijkstra's weakest-precondition calculus, which is integrated into the entire specification-design-implementation process associated with the AMN language.

questions.q: The AMN principle of 'compositional structuring' states what?
o: The combination of abstract machines is also an abstract machine, permitting hierarchical specification
Every machine must be specified in one step
questions.e: AMN's compositional structuring means that the combination of abstract machines is itself an abstract machine, which permits hierarchical specification: large specifications can be constructed from smaller ones.
